what: The keystick in profile: one thickness of wood, and the parts glued to it or cut out of it.

source.instrument: natural keys from a grand piano keyboard

generic_not_a_model: These stand in for a plausible grand rather than describing any maker's key.
the_point_of_this_file: Each feature is recorded with what it is FOR, because the reason is what says where it may be moved. A key read as a stack of steps gets the mass about right and all of that wrong.

records.name: stick_thickness
records.what_for: The keystick's own wood. One piece, one thickness; everything else is glued to it or cut out of it.

records.name: key_length_overall
records.what_for: Tail to the covering's lip, the 2 mm overhang included.

records.name: keytop_thickness
records.what_for: The covering. It sits ON the wood, not in a rebate, so the step a reader sees partway along the key is the covering ending.

records.name: key_front_thickness
records.what_for: The fronton, glued over the end grain. Its outer face is the key front, where key height and key dip are read. Touchweights are referred to the covering's lip instead, keytop_overhang in front of it.

records.name: keytop_overhang
records.what_for: The covering's lip beyond that face. It overhangs the WOOD by 4 mm, of which the fronton takes 2. The lip is the 'front lip of the key' every touchweight's measuring point is taken back from (touchweight-protocol.json), so this is the distance between the touchweight datum and the key height and dip datum.

records.name: capsule_length
records.what_for: More wood where the balance mortise is cut.

records.name: back_check_block_length
records.what_for: Something for the back check wire to be driven into, where the hammer's tail arrives.
records.note: Its length is measured; its place along the key is not. The engine places the block from the balance pin, because the action fixes where the hammer's tail falls and the key's length does not: a key lengthened at the back keeps its block where it stands. The measured section's block has its back end 220 mm behind the balance pin, where the tail measured on this key ends (the tail beginning immediately behind the block, tail_length below): 500 mm from the key's end to the covering's lip, the lip 260 mm in front of the pin, put the key's end 240 mm behind it, and 20 mm of tail end 220 mm behind it. Derived, not measured, and the 260 mm rests on a key front of 258 mm, which has no record: data/profiles/measured-section.json states it as an assumption.

records.name: back_check_block_height
records.note: Taller than the capsule: this is the highest wood on the key.

records.name: tail_length
records.what_for: The tail is cut down to set the height the damper system bears at. It begins immediately behind the back check block.
records.note: Immediately behind the block is what this key shows, and the measured section keeps it. It is not a rule of the engine: a key whose tail ends further back carries the keystick's full height between the tail and the block, and a tail running on under the block is refused.

records.name: tail_underside_rise
records.what_for: The underside is relieved towards the very end so that the key beds FLAT on its back rail cloth. The cloth is a flat strip and the key stands nose-up, so two rigid flats would meet at a corner and the tail would dig in; relieving the underside by the angle the key stands at puts the faces parallel. Owner's account.

records.name: tail_underside_rise_run
records.note: Long and shallow: 2.5 mm over 77 mm is 1.86 degrees. The rest attitude it has to match is 2.26 degrees (a 10.2 mm dip over a 258 mm arm), so on these figures the two do not agree and the key bears on the back edge of its cloth, 0.41 degrees from flat. Both were given as approximate; the bench reports the miss rather than arbitrating. For a 10.2 mm dip the rise would be 3.0 mm over 77, or 2.5 mm over 63.

records.name: capstan_seat
records.what_for: There is none: the capstan screws into a hole bored straight through the keystick, with no pad glued under it.

records.name: capstan_behind_balance_owner
records.note: Measured on the owner's key: a design parameter that varies by maker and by note, and with the key front's place the one that sets the key weight ratio. The measured section's profile places its capstan here, read as a position behind the balance pin. For comparison, Thorin gives 128.7 mm (his thesis, §4.5.2) and 129 mm (his Table 2.1).

records.name: front_mortise_from_front_edge
records.what_for: Where the front mortise is cut, measured back from the key's front edge. Back from the front edge and not forward from the balance pin because that is the dimension the key carries: lengthen a key and its front end and its mortise move together. It is what the frame's front rail is placed from, so it is also what decides whether a rail already bolted down still has a mortise over it.
records.note: Not measured. It is the difference between the two numbers the model held before this one existed - a front edge 258 mm from the balance pin and a front rail pin at 225 - so it reproduces the frame that was there, and nothing more. A calliper from the key's front end to the near side of the mortise would replace it.

records.name: front_mortise_length
records.what_for: The slot's length ALONG the key. Longer than the 5 mm pin standing in it, because the key swings about its balance pin and the mortise travels through a small arc past a pin that does not move. The clearance is also what lets a frame be a few tenths out of place without the key knowing, so it is the tolerance a frame design is judged against.
records.note: Not measured, and not the lateral fit: across the keyboard the mortise is bushed and close on the pin's wide faces, which is what holds the key straight and is not a dimension in the sagittal plane. 8 mm is 3 mm of total slack on a 5 mm pin.

records.name: front_mortise_depth
records.what_for: How far the front mortise reaches up into the key, from its underside: 3 mm of recess, then 19 mm of mortise above it. It is the mortise stop: how far the front rail pin may rise into the key at the bottom of its stroke (key-frame-sections.json, the_pin_must_stay_in_its_mortise).
records.note: Measured by the owner on these keys. The engine draws the mortise as one slot of this depth, open at the underside; the recess and the mortise are not told apart.

materials.statement: The key front and the covering are white. The capsule and the back check block are of a wood different from the keystick's.
materials.what_for: Each piece of the key is drawn as its own part with its own material, so that a reader tells the pieces apart as on a real key. A colour is the view's choice from the material; the material is the model's.

deliberately_absent: The balance mortise. None of its dimensions is measured, and the balance pin's height waits on the same measurement (key-frame-sections.json), so it is not drawn and the balance pin stands hidden in the key's wood, rather than in a hole shaped from a guess. The front mortise is drawn: its depth is measured (front_mortise_depth), and its place and length are the two S records above it.
still_to_measure: Where the capsule sits along the key. It depends on whether the key is a natural or a sharp, and belongs with the balance rail rather than here.

One of these keys weighed whole, as a key that arrives leaded is weighed: its mass on a scale, its front weight on Stanwood's jig, and how far back from the covering's lip the weight was centred. Until then the measured section has no mass and refuses every reading that needs one. It is the entry point of the first validation (docs/FOUNDATIONS.md §5.2 a), and the measurement to ask for first.

Where the key stands along its balance pin: the distance from the centre of the balance hole to the key front, or to the covering's lip. The measured section assumes its key front 258 mm in front of the pin and lays its measured 500 mm back from the lip for its tail; with the capstan measured at 122 mm, that front gives a key weight ratio of 0.494, under the 0.50 to 0.60 published for a natural, so the distance decides the ratio.

The chamfer, which of the three readings it is: 3.0 mm of rise over 77 mm, 2.5 mm over 63 mm, or a key whose dip is really 8.4 mm. The owner's answer - handle the flat case and the edge case rather than forcing the three to agree - is implemented, so nothing is blocked on it; what it decides is whether the measured section beds flat, and it holds 2.5 mm over 77, which is the third reading, beside a 10.2 mm dip, which is not. The bench reports the 0.41 degrees rather than arbitrating.
The front mortise: how far back from the key's front end it is cut, and how long the slot is along the key. Both are S above, and the second is the tolerance a frame design is judged against.
Where the back check block stands along the key, as a distance from the balance pin to its back end. The measured section's 220 mm is where the measured tail ends, derived and not measured.

The clearance cut in the top of the key between the capstan and the back check block, not right behind the capstan: it is there so that the wippen rail, which runs across the keyboard over the keys, cannot rub the key, and behind it the key comes back to its full height, the back check block glued on that. Where its two ends stand, as distances behind the balance pin, and how deep it is cut below the full top. The engine draws such a clearance, placed from the balance pin as the back check block is, since the action places the rail it clears; the measured section's profile states it absent until it is measured.

Where the key's tail bears on the back rail cloth. Asked for and WORTH LESS THAN IT LOOKS, which is why it is last: the regulation solver re-places the punchings on whatever arm the key bears at and meets the targets on each, so sweeping the cloth from 170 to 225 mm behind the balance pin moves the bedding angle by 0.049 degrees and leaves key height and dip on their targets, within the paper the drawer lays them in: a back rail's position is forgiving. The bound is real and the number is not critical.
not_weighed_here: No mass is recorded in this file: a key's mass is not a property of its section. The owner notes that keys differ across the keyboard in shape and in how much wood and lead they carry, so each key is weighed whole, on the bench, and an outline never weighs one.
